catalog_quote: Tuwari does not make use of tone, stress or segment length to distinguish between words. [...] sentences in Tuwari feature an acoustically prominent final syllable. This may be the effect of final lengthening. When one examines spectrograms, no syllable seems to carry special pitch or intensity. [...] A reviewer listened to the text and arrived at a similar conclusion. According to their analysis, stress is often word-final. They also heard secondary stress on every second syllable before main stress. That as may be, stress does not seem to be an important property of the Tuwari word. There are no minimal pairs that are distinguished only by prominence.

new_statements.relation_note: 9 consonants /p t k ɸ s h m n l/, 5 vowels /i ɛ a ɔ u/; glides and [ʔ ʕ] non-phonemic (hiatus resolution); no codas; explicit statements that tone, stress and length are not contrastive and that prominence is word/sentence-final (length).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No lexical tone, no contrastive stress, no contrastive length. Impressionistically the final syllable of the (phonological) word / sentence is the prominent one, realised mainly as extra length with no special pitch or intensity; the authors transcribe and refer to the word-final vowel as 'stressed' (sec. 2.2) but stress 'does not seem to be an important property of the Tuwari word' (no minimal pairs; enclitic particles like /-io/ variably stressed at the phrase edge; apocope deletes final vowels of non-phrase-final words).
new_statements.secondary_stress: A reviewer (not the authors) heard secondary stress on every second syllable before the word-final main stress; authors report no instrumental support.
new_statements.exceptions: Particles, especially /-io/, may be stressed or unstressed at the phrase edge with no pragmatic effect; apocope of final vowels in non-phrase-final words; mid-vowel reduction to [e,o,ə] in non-final (unstressed) position, blocked after [h,q] and before a final stressed mid vowel; no acoustic study undertaken.
new_statements.identity_note: Sec. 1: 'The Tuwari language is a Papuan language spoken by 300 speakers (personal estimate) in the Sandaun province of Papua New Guinea', 12-value gender system, data from Loiseau's 2013-2019 field trips; second author is the sole Tuwari [tww] fieldworker whose HAL records Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description (Loiseau 2022) belongs to. Same languoid as tuwa1242; no namesake issue.

Only a phylum-wide generalisation (p. 732) that Sepik-Ramu Phylum languages mostly show 'lack of complex suprasegmental systems', low vowel inventories and a quasi-phonemic schwa; the Leonhard Schultze section covers lexicostatistics and Pai noun classification only.
